speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: According to international organisations, such as the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and INTERPOL, organised criminal networks are expanding and diversifying their activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Recent terrorist incidents, such as the Paris attacks, have also shown how attackers have been able to plan attacks from abroad and cross borders to carry out their activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As a global financial and transport hub, Singapore is a potential target for organised crime and terrorist groups and a possible conduit for their activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In order to tackle this trend more effectively, governments and law enforcement agencies around the world need to cooperate more closely and intensively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The exchange of information is essential to our international cooperation, crime control and border security efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Having access to information, such as photographs, fingerprints and criminal records, aids our law enforcement agencies in their investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, fingerprints lifted from a crime scene in Singapore can be compared against fingerprint records held by a foreign law enforcement agency to identify potential foreign suspects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Information on the criminal background of an individual also helps investigations, allows law enforcement agencies to identify recalcitrant offenders and facilitates the detection of suspicious persons at border checkpoints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For our law enforcement agencies to ask for and receive such information from our foreign counterparts for the purpose of investigating transnational crime in Singapore, we must be able to reciprocate and share such information in return.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This requirement for reciprocity is a long-established and internationally accepted principle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act (MACMA) enables us to provide a range of assistance to other countries on criminal matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This was amended in 2014 to simplify the conditions which must be satisfied before mutual legal assistance can be rendered and expand the range of offences in respect of which mutual legal assistance may be given or received under that Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our law enforcement agencies also have long-standing arrangements to render assistance to their foreign counterparts at a Police-to-Police level for investigation purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This includes the regular exchange of information, such as criminal records and relevant identifying information, with other law enforcement agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is a common and well-established practice among law enforcement agencies around the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, as a member of INTERPOL, Singapore exchanges information with INTERPOL member countries in accordance with established INTERPOL rules which serve to protect the integrity and confidentiality of the transmitted data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But, in the absence of express legislation, such sharing is heavily circumscribed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, the Page: 76 information generally cannot be adduced as evidence in Court or used for any other purposes besides investigation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, the Bill introduces a new section 13I to allow a Singapore designated authority, namely the Head of the Criminal Records Office, to share information about the individual that is kept on the criminal register with a foreign law enforcement agency, so long as stringent safeguards relating to the retention, use and destruction of the register information are secured through an undertaking given by the foreign law enforcement agency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is similar to the practices of foreign jurisdictions, such as the United Kingdom (UK), Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These would include information, such as the fingerprints and photographs of any person who is convicted of a crime by a Court in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Such a person's conviction in the register must also not have been spent or treated as spent under RCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: What are the safeguards that will be put in place to prevent the wrongful disclosure and abuse of the information?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, sharing will only be permitted for certain specified purposes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Under section 13I, register information will only be shared with a foreign law enforcement agency if the information is requested for the purpose of comparing information transmitted and identifying matches for investigation in certain matters or for proceedings in respect of those matters; or for deciding whether to make a request under MACMA or a requisition under the Extradition Act or for a purpose prescribed under RCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, the foreign law enforcement agency will need to give us an appropriate undertaking in relation to the retention, use and destruction of the register information in order to assure us that the confidentiality of information shared will be adequately protected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The foreign law enforcement agency must also comply with conditions prescribed for transmission of register information and any other conditions that the Singapore-designated authority may impose in relation to the transmission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, if a foreign authority has breached certain conditions in the previous undertaking, Singapore may impose additional procedures to prevent similar occurrences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To aid investigations, RCA currently provides for the taking of registrable particulars, such as fingerprints and body samples of a person accused of a crime but only when he is under arrest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The period for which such a person may be detained in custody without a Magistrate's authority cannot exceed 48 hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is necessary because there are some situations where law enforcement agencies will not have the opportunity to take these fingerprints and samples within 48 hours after arrest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Such a scenario could arise during mass arrests or if an arrested person is warded in hospital for up to 48 hours or longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Under section 68 of the Criminal Procedure Code, Police officers are not permitted to detain a person in custody who has been arrested without a warrant longer than 48 hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This also aligns the position in Singapore with that in foreign jurisdictions such as the UK, where the police may register a person while he is on bail if he has not had his fingerprints or samples taken in the course of investigations, or the fingerprints or samples taken are not suitable or of insufficient quality to allow matching comparison or analysis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I wish to raise some concerns about clause 4 which relates to the furnishing of information on our Register of Criminals to foreign law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, clause 4 enables a Singapore-designated authority to share with a foreign law enforcement agency information about an individual recorded on our Register of Criminals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have noted that clause 4 details safeguards that the Singapore-designated authority should adhere to before deciding to release any information to the foreign law enforcement agency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such safeguards include requiring the foreign agency to give an undertaking in relation to the retention, use and destruction of the register information.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The foreign agency must also undertake that Page: 78 information received from Singapore will be kept and maintained using such methods and technologies that will ensure that unauthorised persons cannot access the information and that the information will not be used for ulterior purposes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the proposed section 13I(4)(6) of the Bill, the Government intends to be able to share information with potentially all countries in the world, since it defines "foreign law enforcement agency" very broadly. "Foreign law enforcement agency" is defined to include agencies in countries that are members of INTERPOL as well as those that are not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: INTERPOL itself consists of 190 member countries, practically all the nations on earth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, in the opening speech, the Senior Minister of State referred to INTERPOL rules, but my question is: how do we know whether these countries can actually fulfil these rules that they have signed up to?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And will we take their word for it, or will more be done to ascertain for ourselves?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, Madam, according to the proposed section 13I(3), the Government actually foresees that a receiving country may breach an undertaking given, and this is rather worrying.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In line with greater ASEAN integration, there have been discussions amongst ASEAN country Ministers about the need for cooperation to combat transnational crime.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Transnational crime in ASEAN is understood to refer to drug trafficking, terrorism, economic crimes, human trafficking, money laundering, piracy, weapon smuggling and cybercrime and, since 2015, includes illicit trafficking of wildlife and timber, and people smuggling.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Last year, Singapore signed up to the Kuala Lumpur Declaration on Combating Transnational Crime, which calls for a new ASEAN Plan of Action to Combat Transnational Crime and greater information sharing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With this backdrop, I would have presumed that if a request for register information came from an ASEAN country, it would be contrary to ASEAN integration to reject the request.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is with these considerations in mind that I rise in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Page: 79 Under the RCA, the Police are able to keep records in the Register of persons convicted of any crime specified in the First and Second Schedules of the Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Particulars, such as the photograph, finger impressions and conviction records, are recorded.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Register of Criminals is useful in Police investigations, especially in the identification of suspects.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By having access to fingerprints or DNA of persons that have been convicted of scheduled crimes, the Police may be able to expedite their investigations if they are able to find a match between evidence found as part of their investigations and those on the Register.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When RCA was last amended in 2005, it was amended to help former offenders to reintegrate into society by allowing those who have criminal records that have been "spent" to be deemed to have no record of that conviction if they are able to satisfy a five-year crime-free period.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Likewise, the proposed amendments to RCA that are before the House this afternoon are timely and equally important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the increasing links among countries, we are witnessing unprecedented levels of connectivity in our globalised world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result of this increased connectivity, we are also experiencing an increase in transnational crimes across borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to voice some advantages of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the proposed amendments will facilitate the sharing of information among our Home Team and foreign law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will enable us to deal with the scourge of transnational crime and terrorist groups more effectively and expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And to prevent any abuse or the wrongful disclosure of the information shared, foreign law enforcement agencies will be required to undertake to protect the confidentiality of the information shared and to only use the information for crime prevention, criminal investigation or related proceedings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Singapore-designated authority would even have the ability to suspend the transmission of information about an individual if that authority is of the opinion that the foreign law enforcement agency has failed to comply with the undertaking that it had given and does not take steps to rectify the non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, our Home Team will also be able to request reciprocal assistance from law enforcement agencies when investigating and prosecuting criminals in Singapore, through a crime prevention exchange of information arrangement with other foreign law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will strengthen Singapore's ability to pursue criminals who operate beyond national boundaries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important in light of the establishment of the INTERPOL Global Complex for Innovation in Singapore in 2014.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the increasingly fast-paced criminal landscape, local and foreign enforcement agencies must ensure that there is a collaborative framework in place to facilitate the timely exchange of vital information and intelligence, so that we are able to deal with transnational crimes quickly and effectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, or second advantage, the proposed amendments will also strengthen operational procedures for the registration of criminals in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may hinder the conduct of a thorough investigation by the Police where a crime has been committed and the Police are conducting their investigations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It bears noting that there are already safeguards which may help ensure that these proposed augmented powers of the Police to obtain "registrable particulars" or body samples are Page: 80 not abused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Registrar will then be required to destroy the finger impressions, photographs and registrable particulars that were obtained pursuant to RCA and to immediately remove the DNA information of that person from the DNA database.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, I have a series of questions here.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What if investigations cease before acquittal or before the case gets to Court?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or what if there is a long delay in investigations?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or if investigations are put on hold for an unduly long period of time?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Should not the registrable particulars and the like be destroyed in these situations also?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ultimately, a collaborative approach to investigation and information sharing is essential if we want to be able to deal with transnational crimes quickly, decisively and effectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Madam, it is equally important to emphasise that it is also incumbent on the Police and the authorities to ensure that such private information is not abused or illegitimately utilised.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In today's porous, globally-connected world where terrorism has cast a growing shadow on lives worldwide, sharing criminal records across borders fulfils a basic security need.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Take the Paris terror attacks, which killed 130 people, as an example.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The day after the gun and suicide-bomb attacks, one of the suspects who survived was stopped by the French police but was later released.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Belgian police had, unfortunately, failed to share with their French counterparts about the information that this man was a known radical who had tried to travel to Syria to fight for the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, or ISIS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The man is still on the run today.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Closer to home, in Indonesia, several militant groups have pledged allegiance to ISIS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In January, at least eight people were killed in an ISIS-perpetrated attack near a Jakarta shopping mall.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Malaysian authorities have foiled several ISIS-inspired attack plots and arrested several persons involved in ISIS activities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Just last week, the Australian government indicated that terrorists may be planning attacks in Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, given this scenario, the sharing of criminal records, fingerprints and photographs across borders will make it harder for terrorists and criminals to travel under false identities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Cross-border cooperation does not just address concerns over terrorism, but also online commercial crime, Page: 81 money laundering and other transnational crimes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In Europe, the European Criminal Records Information System (ECRIS) was set up in 2012 to allow courts and law enforcement agencies to obtain criminal records from other European Union (EU) member states.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the wake of the Paris terror attacks, it was announced in January 2016 that ECRIS will be further expanded to include the fingerprints of non-EU citizens.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The list of suspects will be used by security officials at all entry points in Malaysia as well as across the US.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Transnational cooperation is a step in the right direction towards the prevention of global crime.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that Singapore enjoys a close working relationship with INTERPOL, as said by the Senior Minister of State, and MHA has set up units to facilitate international exchange.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For instance, the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO) within the Commercial Affairs Department shares financial intelligence with foreign counterparts if they had signed memoranda of understanding, while the Singapore Police Force's International Cooperation Department facilitates cooperation and information exchange with foreign counterparts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to clarify with the Senior Minister of State how the proposed amendment Bill ties in with Singapore's international working arrangements with INTERPOL, and various other platforms which already exist for information exchange on global crimes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How many countries have similar provisions that can share their criminal records with Singapore besides the US, the UK, Australia and New Zealand mentioned by the Senior Minister of State earlier on?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does it mean that no other ASEAN countries have a similar provision to share the information with Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In addition, I would like to request the Senior Minister of State to elaborate more on the safeguards to prevent abuse and to protect the interests of Singaporeans under the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The last thing we want is for a Singaporean with decades-old criminal records of petty crimes to have his history made known to the immigration officer at an immigration checkpoint of a foreign country, thereby subjecting him to unnecessary body and bag checks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, we would like to know when, what and how the criminal records would be shared with other countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will the exchange of criminal records be shared on a request-only basis?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Singapore, as mentioned, has focused very much on the rehabilitation and re-integration of offenders into the society.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Yellow Ribbon Project has made much progress in recent years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I am very glad that the Senior Minister of State has confirmed that criminal records that had been rendered spent will be not be shared with other countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But does it mean that all other records, beside those spent, in the Register of Criminals will be shared with other countries?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, how will the criminal records be shared with other countries?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will it be via a shared platform like ECRIS?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If this is so, we could have a problem of different countries tracking different things to different degrees and for different lengths of time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, when the EU adopted ECRIS, it became apparent that Britain hangs on to the most minor convictions for years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a result, local jobseekers could not apply for "sensitive" jobs Page: 82 like teachers and policemen while migrants from other EU countries go to England and apply for these jobs because their countries wiped the slate clean or did not keep records of low-level offences.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Clearly, the "seriousness" and treatment of crimes are regarded differently across borders and this constitutes a problem.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The implications could be even more acute if Singaporeans are residing in countries with high 99% or higher conviction in the court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, Singaporeans deserve to know in detail what, when and how information is shared with a foreign country to prevent abuse so as not to disadvantage Singaporeans unnecessarily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: All three have raised a couple of questions which I will seek to address.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, Madam, Mr Ang asked how the RCA amendments would complement existing working arrangements that we currently have with other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singapore relies on a combination of formal and informal cooperation channels to exchange information with foreign counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I had mentioned earlier the Act known as MACMA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This provides a formal channel through which law enforcement agencies render legal assistance to foreign law enforcement agencies with respect to any criminal matter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, for instance, under MACMA, you can ask for the collection of evidence, search and seizure, freezing of accounts, arrangements for witnesses to be made available to give evidence and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But beyond the MACMA framework for formal assistance, our law enforcement agencies can also render assistance informally either through INTERPOL, which most countries are members of, as Ms Sylvia Lim pointed out, or directly with our foreign counterparts through Police-to-Police contacts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, any request for register information has to be assessed on a case-by-case basis for public interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, register information can be shared to help identify suspects in time-critical investigations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Bill also expressly allows register information to be shared as a precursor to a request for more formal assistance under MACMA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In other words, the Bill, which amends RCA, will complement the MACMA process and Page: 83 strengthen our fight against transnational crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members also asked about the mechanics of sharing register information with foreign counterparts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, in a sense, it addresses partly what Mr Ang and Ms Sylvia Lim have asked.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the proposed amendments, a foreign law enforcement agency may request register information for certain purposes specified in the Act, which I have just mentioned earlier, one of which is to compare the register information with information held by the foreign law enforcement agency to identify suspects involved in the investigation of a matter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Exchange of information can also be made to prevent crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Depending on the arrangement between Singapore and the foreign law enforcement agency, the Singapore-designated authority, or the head of CRO, may be able to share register information pursuant to the arrangement even in the absence of a specific request for the transmission of that information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A Singapore- designated authority may share such information to assist a foreign law enforcement agency in investigating or prosecuting foreign offences, particularly serious criminal or terrorist offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even then, register information will be shared on a limited basis and foreign agencies will, certainly, not get unfettered access to all our data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With regard to the transmission of register information in relation to the investigation of a foreign offence or an investigation to prevent the commission of a foreign offence, I should highlight that the Bill provides a definition of what a foreign offence is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in this way, this ensures that information is not disclosed for non-serious or trivial matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I would also like to assure Mr Ang Wei Neng that the register information to be shared will not include spent criminal records.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I come now to the nub of Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Ang's concerns, which are principally about safeguards to be imposed and the concern about whether our counterparts will adhere to the conditions that they have agreed to and the undertakings they have given and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Before I go into the details, it is important to recognise the balance that we seek to strike here.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the one hand, we are certainly very concerned about the confidentiality of information, the identifiable information, names, photographs, fingerprints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But equally of concern is the need for law enforcement agencies around the world to get up to pace in terms of international cooperation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Crime knows no boundaries with the Internet, with travel being so easy and with borders being relatively porous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Transnational organised crime sometimes leads governments and foreign law enforcement agencies to scuttle around to try to nip the problem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, cooperation is essential, otherwise, we fall behind the curve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Ang and Ms Sylvia Lim raised challenges and concerns regarding the sharing of information or data on certain shared platforms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Ang mentioned ECRIS, and we are mindful of this and are careful to ensure that procedures and the infrastructure of all parties concerned protect the confidentiality of the information transmitted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will certainly not deposit register information on such a shared platform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, in order to allow the sharing of register information between Singapore and a foreign law enforcement agency, that agency must give us an appropriate undertaking to use the information disclosed only for a specified purpose listed under the Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Requests that are made in a broad or tenuous manner, or by way of a "fishing expedition", will not be acceded to or entertained.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Foreign law enforcement agencies should also never use our records for such irrelevant purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Should they do so or breach any of the terms of the undertaking, there will be consequences, as I will explain shortly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Members asked whether a past criminal record of petty crime would expose a Singaporean to undue security checks at overseas border checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I believe Mr Ang Wei Neng did ask that at the end of his speech.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Every country, including us in Singapore, has its own entry requirements to prevent, deter and detect undesirable individuals entering their country.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singaporeans seeking to enter a foreign country must meet the country's entry requirements, which may include holding a valid passport or entry visa.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ultimately, a foreign country retains the right to impose conditions or refuse entry to migrants at the checkpoint.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, the foreign law enforcement agency is also required to undertake to protect the confidentiality of information by ensuring that the information is kept and maintained using methods and technologies that ensure that unauthorised persons cannot access the information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A Singapore-designated authority will be able to refuse further transmission of register information to a foreign agency if the Singapore-designated authority is of the opinion that the foreign law enforcement agency has breached such an undertaking and has not taken steps to rectify the non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, the foreign law enforcement agency must be able to comply with conditions prescribed for the transmission of register information under the Act and any other conditions that the Singapore authority may impose, especially in relation to the transmission.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes complying with any request by Singapore to delete or update the records if a criminal conviction has been rendered spent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These safeguards will ensure that any exchange of information is limited to countries that ensure the confidentiality of information exchanged and prevent its unauthorised use.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the course of her speech, Ms Sylvia Lim noted all these safeguards, but her concern was how we will ensure on a practical basis that these safeguards are met.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She also mentioned that the membership of INTERPOL covers much of the globe and we are all party to this international co-operation arrangement for law enforcement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While the Act does appear to allow us to share information with all these countries and more, the reality is that by striking that balance between the need for cooperation and privacy, Singapore will conduct its due diligence in working out arrangements, ensuring undertakings are made, given and also able to be abided by and audited.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is not something that can be done overnight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It Page: 85 involves agencies knowing one another, meeting one another, having lots of discussions about the safeguards that need to be put in place, the software, systems, audit mechanisms that need to be ensured, in order to ensure that level of trust to allow us to share information expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sharing information quickly will help us to deter, prevent and, ultimately, solve crimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I believe Mr Christopher de Souza did ask a question about the taking of photographs and fingerprints of a person accused of crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under the current Act, it would be when a person is under arrest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Under this Bill, we seek to expand it to when a person is on bail or when the person is given a personal bond, and I believe Members who have spoken understand the necessity of having this mechanism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But Mr de Souza's concern is: what if a person's case has been put into abeyance for some time, or if the trial is particularly long or has been set for a date far into the future?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Is it fair that the data is kept on the register?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If we look at section 4 of the Act, section 4 would not be touched.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Section 4 states that the Register of Criminals is kept for persons who are convicted of crimes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While the fingerprints and photographs may have been taken at the point of arrest, they will not be recorded on the register.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It will only be recorded when the case has been completed or if a person has been convicted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, I hope that this assures the Member that it will not unduly compromise the persons in Singapore whose trials may take a little longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To be effective against such threats, we must have greater cooperation in the information exchange among law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I would like him to clarify whether this ongoing process applies also to our ASEAN counterparts or has that already been finalised and it is quite clear that we are confident that we can share information with our ASEAN counterparts without needing to go through this because it has been done earlier.
